title: Garter stitch baby blanket
subtitle: A straight single-panel rectangle in all-garter DK, sized for a cot.
excerpt: A 75 by 90 cm baby blanket worked flat from cast-on to cast-off in plain garter stitch on 4 mm needles, using approximately 250 g of machine-washable DK. Garter stitch lies flat without blocking, which suits a first blanket project.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 3rd series (1887), §Knitted Blankets and Covers, describes single-panel garter-stitch cot blankets as a standard nursery knit. The construction is unchanged: cast on for the width, work in garter stitch to the desired length, cast off.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 44 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: The simplest knitted fabric: knit every stitch on every row when working flat. Both sides look identical, with horizontal ridges. Lies flat without blocking and has more lengthwise stretch than stocking stitch.

A two-strand cast-on that produces a neat, elastic foundation row. The yarn is looped over the thumb and index finger; each stitch is formed in one motion. Faster than the knitted-on cast-on once the technique is familiar.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle in DK wool, worked flat in
garter stitch
from cast-on to cast-off, finishing at 75 cm wide and 90 cm long.

Single-panel construction suits a baby blanket because there are no seams to come undone in the wash, no ends to weave in on every square, and no shaping to track. Garter stitch was chosen here over stocking stitch because it lies flat without any pressing or blocking: the ridges on both faces hold the edges naturally, so the blanket is cot-ready straight off the needles. Budget about 250 g (about 550 m / 600 yards) of superwash DK wool or a DK wool-cotton blend. Buy everything in matched dye lots. A blanket this size needs two or three full skeins, and a dye-lot shift partway through the blanket is the most common knitting-blanket disappointment. Drape it across a pram or lie it flat in a cot; it folds to a small square for a changing bag.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 250 g (about 550 m / 600 yards) of DK-weight machine-washable yarn
items.substitutions: Superwash merino, superwash wool-cotton blend, or a 100% cotton DK. Avoid non-superwash wool for a baby blanket: standard wool felts in the wash.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) straight or circular needle, 80 cm or longer

items.name: Tapestry needle
items.qty: 1, for weaving in the cast-on and cast-off tails

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked. Work a 15 cm square swatch, leave it flat overnight, then measure the centre 10 cm. Garter stitch does not change much after washing, so you can measure it dry.

If your gauge is 20 stitches per 10 cm instead of 22, the finished blanket will be about 82 cm wide instead of 75 cm at the same 165-stitch cast-on. If your gauge is 24 stitches per 10 cm, the width will be about 69 cm. Move up or down one needle size and re-swatch. A blanket that turns out 5 cm narrower than planned is still usable; a hat that goes wrong wastes far less yarn but matters more for fit.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on
Using the
long-tail cast-on

, cast on 165 stitches. For the long-tail cast-on, you need a tail long enough to form all the stitches. Use the formula: tail length in cm = (needle diameter in mm × stitch count) divided by 10, plus 15 cm for security. For 165 stitches on 4 mm needles: (4 × 165) / 10 + 15 = 66 + 15 = 81 cm. Measure out at least 90 cm of tail before starting; round up to 110 cm to be comfortable. A blanket cast-on is long enough that an under-counted tail forces an unravelling and restart.
Body
Knit every row. That is the whole pattern.

Work until the blanket measures 90 cm from the cast-on edge. At gauge, that is 396 rows total, but measuring is more reliable than counting: lay the blanket flat on a table, smooth it without stretching, and measure from the cast-on ridge to the needle.
When you set this aside, jot the row number or place a locking stitch marker on the current row. The pattern resumes cleanly from any point.
Stitch count check-ins

At row 198 (halfway, about 45 cm): count across the needle. You should have 165 stitches. If the count has drifted, you have either accidentally added a stitch by knitting into the bar between two stitches, or dropped a stitch and it has run down a row. Catching this at the halfway mark costs much less than finding it at the cast-off.
At row 392 (before cast-off, about 89 cm): count again. You should still have 165 stitches. If the count is correct, cast off on the next row.
Common faults

Stitch count creeping up over many rows: an extra stitch is usually added by knitting into the bar between the first and second stitch on the left needle at the start of a row, or by carrying the yarn over the needle before the first stitch. Count every 20 rows until the habit is resolved.

Cast-on edge noticeably tighter than the body: the long-tail cast-on was worked with the working tension rather than a relaxed tension. To avoid this, hold the yarn loosely and let each stitch sit with a small gap around the needle as it forms. Alternatively, cast on over two needles held together, then remove one before knitting the first row.

Dye-lot shift visible mid-blanket: skeins from different dye lots were not alternated. The shift shows as a horizontal line and cannot be disguised after the fact. To avoid it, buy all skeins at once in matched dye lots, or alternate two skeins every two rows so any drift averages out and is invisible to the eye.
Cast-off

Cast off knitwise with a relaxed tension. Work each cast-off stitch as k2, pass the first stitch over the second and off the needle, repeat to the end. Pull each stitch slightly loose as you go: a tight cast-off pulls the top edge inward and makes the blanket narrower at one end than the other.
Finishing

Weave in the two ends (cast-on tail and cast-off tail) on the wrong side using the tapestry needle, running each tail along a garter ridge for at least 5 cm and changing direction once so the yarn cannot pull out. Trim the excess. Garter stitch does not need blocking to lie flat, but a gentle hand wash and flat dry will even out any uneven tension rows.
Care

Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle if the yarn label permits. Superwash merino and DK cotton blends tolerate this well. Do not tumble dry: lay flat on a towel and reshape while damp. If the blanket stretches out of shape over time, wash and lay flat to its original dimensions while wet, then leave to dry.
What to try next

The natural extension of a plain garter blanket is a striped version: switch colour every two rows and carry the unused yarn up the side edge. The construction is identical, so no new technique is needed. After that, a basket-weave or seed-stitch baby blanket uses the same cast-on count and needle size but alternates knit and purl stitches to build texture.
